headline: Big Tech profits from AI, while S&P 493 sees no financial returns, Apollo report finds
summary: Apollo's Daily Spark analysis shows the Magnificent Seven widening their revenue-per-employee lead over the S&P 493, highlighting a growing productivity gap. Most S&P 500 companies show no comparable gains despite heavy AI investment.
details: Apollo data reveals a widening revenue-per-employee gap between the "Magnificent Seven" tech giants and the rest of the S&P 500 (S&P 493) from 2019 to 2026. This highlights a growing productivity disparity, with Big Tech cashing in on AI while others see no financial returns.

Apollo Global Management chief economist Torsten Slok's analysis found no clear evidence that AI is boosting productivity growth outside of the tech sector. He stated that despite massive investments and hype, AI has delivered "zero financial payoff to corporate America outside of tech."

Running AI models at scale often drives up costs due to token usage, turning AI spending into a cost center for many mainstream companies. Established businesses have less incentive to pay for expensive new models if cheaper alternatives suffice.

This creates a challenge for AI providers, as customers require measurable gains in productivity, revenue, or reduced operating costs to sustain their AI investments. Without these benefits, rising AI expenses could negatively impact profit margins.

Slok also noted that AI adoption remains concentrated among a small group of companies. Unless its usage spreads and produces tangible results across more industries, AI's overall economic impact may remain limited.

A PwC India survey in the fintech sector echoed these findings, with 84% of respondents reporting no measurable financial results from their AI investments. Despite this, 48% still prioritize proprietary AI, and many expect AI agents to drive customer experience and cost reduction.

headline: 4 Ray-Ban Meta privacy settings you should change before wearing them
summary: Meta's smart glasses collect various data, from voice interactions to visual AI requests. Understanding and adjusting these settings can help you control what information is shared and stored.
details: Ray-Ban Meta glasses continuously collect data, from listening for the "Hey Meta" wake phrase to processing visual AI requests. Users have options to manage what information is gathered and stored by Meta.

One key area is voice activation. While convenient, the glasses are always listening for "Hey Meta" when enabled, and in the US, Meta stores recordings of AI voice interactions in the cloud, which users must manually delete.

To disable voice activation, connect your glasses to your phone, open the Meta AI app, select your glasses, then go to Meta AI > "Hey Meta" preferences and deactivate the toggle. The touchpad can still activate the assistant.

Cloud media is another setting to review. Enabling it allows Meta to keep copies of photos and videos captured with your glasses on its servers for up to 30 days, even if you intend to import them to your phone.

You can turn off Cloud media in the Meta AI app under Glasses privacy > Cloud media. Disabling this means losing cloud-based features like voice-controlled photo sharing and autocapture, but you can still take and import media.
Meta also collects "additional data," which includes usage analytics on how you use features and how often. This data helps Meta understand product usage but is optional for users to share.

To stop sharing additional data, open the Meta AI app, select your glasses, then go to Glasses privacy > Share additional data and toggle it off. This setting does not affect how you use photos, calls, or music.
Finally, visual data from AI experiences, such as asking the assistant to identify objects, can be stored for AI training. This is separate from gallery photos and is subject to its own opt-out.

To prevent Meta from storing visual data from AI experiences, go to your glasses' settings in the Meta AI app, select Meta AI, and disable "Store visual data from AI experiences." Your glasses must be out of their case for this.

Even with these settings adjusted, Meta continues to collect data necessary for device operation and safety, and voice commands/AI requests are governed by specific guidelines. Turning off data sharing does not delete previously collected information.
